scenario: Security Hub flags versioning as disabled on an S3 bucket used by the biomedical research team. The bucket stores synthetic patient datasets used for federated learning model training across hospital networks. The datasets are regenerated from Synthea every sprint cycle. Versioning is intentionally disabled because previous versions have no recovery value — all datasets are deterministically reproducible from Synthea configuration files.
why_misclassified: The scanner flags absent versioning on a bucket tagged data_type=patient_records without detecting that the records are synthetic (EC-21). Synthea-generated data has no versioning requirement since it can be regenerated deterministically.
detection_signal: Security Hub S3.14: S3 buckets should use versioning. Bucket: federated-learning-training-data-prod. Tags: data_type=patient_records.
ground_truth: All data synthetic (Synthea v3.2). data_type=patient_records tag is inaccurate — applied before synthetic classification was established. No PHI. Deterministic regeneration makes versioning unnecessary.
remediation_impact: Enabling versioning on a large synthetic training data bucket incurs significant S3 storage costs for previous versions of multi-GB datasets with no data recovery benefit.

scenario: Defender for Cloud flags Azure SQL Server auditing as disabled on a SQL server in the healthcare tenant. The SQL server hosts only the legacy benefits administration database that was migrated to Azure SQL Managed Instance 4 months ago. The original SQL server is in a decommissioned state — the resource still exists in the subscription pending deletion sign-off from legal.
why_misclassified: EC-11: Sunset resource. The SQL server is decommissioned (no active databases, no connections) and the data it hosted has been migrated. The auditing gap is on an inactive, data-free resource.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: Azure SQL Server 'legacy-benefits-sql-prod' auditing not configured. Severity: HIGH. Subscription: healthcare-prod.
ground_truth: SQL Server legacy-benefits-sql-prod: no active databases, no connections in 4 months. Data migrated to SQL MI benefits-mi-prod. Resource exists pending legal deletion approval (same pattern as EC-11).
remediation_impact: Configuring auditing on a decommissioned server with no data is wasted effort. Deletion should proceed once legal approval is obtained.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a service account key for the FHIR bulk export process as not rotated within 90 days. The service account key is created fresh at the start of each bulk export run (a quarterly process), used for the 2-4 hour export window, and then deleted immediately after the export completes. The current finding was triggered because the key created for the current quarter's export was detected mid-export.
why_misclassified: EC-10: Ephemeral key created for a time-bounded job. The scanner detected the key during the 4-hour export window without recognizing it as a short-lived, per-run key that will be deleted on completion.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: Service account key for fhir-bulk-export@healthcare-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com age > 90 days. (Scanner misread creation date due to UTC offset). Category: SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY_NOT_ROTATED.
ground_truth: Key created at export start (2025-02-01T08:00:00Z). Export in progress. Key will be deleted at export completion (estimated 2025-02-01T12:00:00Z). Per-run ephemeral key lifecycle. UTC offset calculation error in scanner caused false 90-day age reading.
remediation_impact: Deleting the key mid-export aborts the quarterly FHIR bulk export job, requiring restart and data reconciliation. The key is already being managed correctly.

scenario: Defender for Cloud flags an NSG on the hospital's HL7 ADT listener server as allowing inbound 2575 (HL7 MLLP) from any source. An Azure DDoS Network Protection plan and an Azure Firewall policy with application rules restrict all inbound 2575 traffic to source IP ranges from partner sending systems. The NSG rule appears open but the upstream Azure Firewall policy enforces the actual IP restriction.
why_misclassified: EC-17 analog for Azure Firewall: The scanner evaluates the NSG in isolation without detecting the upstream Azure Firewall policy that enforces the actual IP-based restriction. Azure Firewall policies are evaluated before NSG rules.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: NSG 'hl7-listener-nsg-prod' allows Any:2575 inbound. Severity: HIGH. Category: NETWORK_EXPOSURE.
ground_truth: Azure Firewall Policy rule collection: Allow 2575 from [partner-hospital-ips]. Deny 2575 from Any (higher priority). NSG is a secondary control. Azure Firewall is the primary enforcement point for MLLP source restriction.
remediation_impact: Restricting the NSG to match the Firewall policy is good defense-in-depth but adds maintenance overhead when partner hospital IPs change — they must be updated in both Firewall policy and NSG.

scenario: A GCP Cloud Storage bucket containing surgical consent forms (scanned PDFs with patient signatures, diagnosis, procedure details) has allUsers read access. The bucket is tagged data_type=documents and a CSPM suppression rule exempts documents buckets from public-access checks because the document management team claimed all documents are de-identified templates. The tag was applied to all buckets in the documents project without validating actual content.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Tag-based suppression based on a bulk tag application without content validation. The data_type=documents tag was intended for document templates but was applied to all buckets in the project, including those with PHI-containing patient consent forms.
detection_signal: CSPM suppression: bucket 'surgical-consents-prod' tag data_type=documents matches suppression rule. GCP SCC finding PUBLIC_BUCKET_ACL suppressed. Actual content: 12,000 signed surgical consent PDFs with full PHI.
ground_truth: Bucket contains 12,000 scanned patient surgical consent forms. PHI includes: patient name, DOB, MRN, procedure name, surgeon name, diagnosis. allUsers read access means any internet user can list and download these forms.
remediation_impact: Immediate: remove allUsers IAM binding, audit GCP storage access logs for unauthorized reads, notify privacy officer, assess HIPAA breach notification obligation under 45 CFR §164.402.

scenario: Defender for Cloud shows an EHR application server VM as fully patched based on its last assessment 60 days ago. A critical OS vulnerability (CVE-2024-21412 — Windows SmartScreen bypass, CVSS 8.1) was published 45 days ago and actively exploited in healthcare sector attacks per CISA KEV. The VM's assessment cycle missed this CVE because the assessment frequency is configured for 60-day intervals.
why_misclassified: EC-24: Stale scan — 60-day assessment interval means a 45-day-old critical CVE that appears in CISA KEV goes undetected until the next assessment cycle. The finding shows NONE because the last scan predates the CVE publication.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: VM 'ehr-app-server-01' vulnerability assessment: 0 CRITICAL (last scan 60 days ago). CVE-2024-21412 (published 45 days ago) not in assessment results.
ground_truth: VM running Windows Server 2022, unpatched for CVE-2024-21412. CISA KEV listed (active exploitation). Assessment cycle: 60 days. CVE published after last assessment. 45-day blind spot for CISA KEV vulnerabilities.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) reduce Defender assessment cycle to 7 days for CISA KEV CVEs, (2) apply Windows Security Update for CVE-2024-21412, (3) review IDS logs for exploitation attempts.

scenario: A CSPM rule for S3 public access checks the bucket-level Block Public Access setting and finds it enabled (BlockPublicAcls=true, BlockPublicPolicy=true). The finding is marked NONE. However, a Lambda function with s3:PutBucketAcl permissions recently applied a public-read ACL to a specific prefix using a signed request that bypassed the bucket-level block. The bucket policy allows a specific Lambda role to use s3:PutBucketAcl, and that role was compromised.
why_misclassified: EC-04: A dead/unexpected code path became active via credential compromise. The scanner checks Block Public Access settings but a Lambda role with s3:PutBucketAcl can override them for specific objects. The scanner does not detect object-level ACL overrides.
detection_signal: CSPM: S3 bucket phi-records-prod BlockPublicAcls=true, BlockPublicPolicy=true. Finding: NONE (compliant). Object-level ACLs on prefix /exports/* set to public-read via compromised Lambda role.
ground_truth: Bucket-level Block Public Access is set. However, a compromised Lambda role (phi-export-lambda-role with s3:PutBucketAcl) applied public-read ACL to 847 objects in the /exports/* prefix. Those objects are publicly readable despite bucket-level settings.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) revoke compromised Lambda role credentials, (2) enumerate and reset all object ACLs in /exports/* prefix, (3) enable S3 Object Ownership=BucketOwnerEnforced to disable all ACLs, (4) rotate Lambda execution role credentials.

scenario: A CSPM scanner's GCP IAM privilege escalation check was disabled 6 months ago due to high false-positive rates in the genomics research project. An external attacker who compromised a researcher's service account has used the existing roles/editor binding to create a new service account key, add roles/owner to the new account, and establish persistence. The disabled check means the privilege escalation path is completely invisible.
why_misclassified: EC-03: Disabled check creating systematic blind spot. The IAM escalation check was disabled globally due to FP tuning issues, removing detection for all IAM privilege escalation paths across all GCP projects.
detection_signal: CSPM scanner: IAM_PRIVILEGE_ESCALATION_CHECK disabled (config: skip_iam_escalation=true). Active attack: roles/owner granted to attacker SA genomics-attacker@genomics-research.iam.gserviceaccount.com. No finding generated.
ground_truth: Attacker has roles/owner on genomics-research-prod project with access to 15TB of patient genomic data. Attack chain: compromised SA -> roles/editor -> create SA key -> add roles/owner -> establish persistence. Completely invisible due to disabled check.
remediation_impact: Immediate IR: (1) revoke all SA keys for compromised account, (2) audit IAM binding changes in Cloud Audit Logs for past 6 months, (3) re-enable IAM escalation check with proper tuning rather than disabling, (4) assess PHI exposure.

scenario: GuardDuty generates a LOW finding for CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B on an EHR application server. A CSPM suppression rule downgrades all CryptoCurrency findings on tagged production servers to LOW because previous findings were false positives from legitimate blockchain health record pilots. The current detection is genuine — an attacker has implanted a cryptominer after exploiting a web application vulnerability, using the same C2 IP pattern as the blockchain pilot but at 10x normal CPU utilization.
why_misclassified: EC-50: Overly broad suppression rule based on prior FP patterns. The rule suppresses all cryptocurrency findings on production servers, including genuine cryptomining that indicates a compromised production EHR server with potential access to PHI.
detection_signal: GuardDuty: CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B on ehr-app-prod-03. Suppression rule applied: tag phi_scope=true + CryptoCurrency finding = downgrade to LOW. CPU utilization: 98% (baseline: 35%).
ground_truth: EC2 instance ehr-app-prod-03: compromised via web app RCE. Cryptominer implanted. CPU 98% (3x normal). Network connections to known mining pool IPs. Instance has database credentials in memory. PHI database accessible from this host.
remediation_impact: Immediate IR: isolate instance, capture memory forensics, rotate all database credentials from this host, review web application logs for exploitation entry point. PHI access audit required.

scenario: A tag-based exemption (data_type=imaging_templates) suppresses public access checks for an Azure Storage account. The account was originally used for radiology report templates (de-identified). A Terraform module change 5 months ago accidentally targeted this storage account for the DICOM image upload pipeline, writing thousands of patient DICOM files to it. The original exemption remains active, hiding the PHI exposure.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Suppression rule based on original data classification that no longer reflects actual content after an infrastructure change. Terraform module drift caused PHI to land in a storage account with a permissive suppression tag.
detection_signal: CSPM suppression: storage account 'radiology-templates-prod' tag data_type=imaging_templates. Public access check suppressed. Actual content: 8,200 patient DICOM files uploaded by misconfigured pipeline (past 5 months).
ground_truth: Storage account contains 8,200 DICOM files with patient identifiers embedded in DICOM headers (patient name, DOB, MRN, study description). allow_blob_public_access=true. Public internet can enumerate and download these files.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) set allow_blob_public_access=false, (2) audit Azure Storage logs for anonymous DICOM downloads, (3) fix Terraform module target, (4) notify privacy officer for breach assessment, (5) inventory exposed DICOM metadata.

scenario: GCP SCC VM Manager (OS patch compliance) shows a hospital administrative server as fully compliant. The server has been in an OS maintenance exclusion window for 90 days due to application stability testing. A HIGH CVE (CVE-2023-4911, glibc Looney Tunables) was published 75 days ago. The maintenance exclusion prevents both patching and scanning, creating a 75-day window where the server is vulnerable and undetected.
why_misclassified: EC-24: Stale scan compounded by maintenance exclusion. The maintenance exclusion prevents scanning, making the compliance report show the last clean scan state (from before the CVE was published) as the current state.
detection_signal: GCP SCC VM Manager: Instance ehr-admin-server-prod — OS patch compliance: COMPLIANT (last scan: 92 days ago, predates CVE-2023-4911 publication by 17 days).
ground_truth: Instance running RHEL 8.6 with glibc 2.34 — vulnerable to CVE-2023-4911 (Looney Tunables, local privilege escalation). CVE published 75 days ago. Maintenance exclusion prevents both scanning and patching. 75-day undetected exposure.
remediation_impact: Immediate: end maintenance exclusion window, apply glibc patch (glibc >= 2.34-60.el8_8.3), trigger compliance rescan. Review maintenance exclusion policy to ensure it does not block vulnerability scanning for CISA KEV items.

scenario: Defender for Cloud Dependency Scanning shows zero vulnerabilities for a hospital's patient portal Azure App Service. The application uses a private NuGet package (HospitalCommon.Auth 3.2.1) from the internal Azure DevOps artifact feed. The package contains a hardcoded JWT signing key left by a developer (a common secret injection bug in internal packages). Since it's a private package not in any public vulnerability database, no CVE exists and no scanner flags it.
why_misclassified: EC-01: Ghost/private package vulnerability. The secret injection in the internal NuGet package has no CVE entry because it was never reported to a public vulnerability database. Standard CVE scanners have zero visibility into private artifact feeds.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: App Service 'patient-portal-prod' — 0 CRITICAL, 0 HIGH dependency vulnerabilities. Package HospitalCommon.Auth 3.2.1 in private feed — no CVE entry.
ground_truth: HospitalCommon.Auth 3.2.1 contains hardcoded JWT signing key (string literal in source). Any application using this package can forge JWT tokens for any user in the hospital system. Package in use by 7 internal applications. Discovered via code review, not scanner.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) rotate JWT signing key across all 7 affected applications, (2) invalidate all active JWT tokens (force re-login), (3) publish HospitalCommon.Auth 3.2.2 with removed hardcoded key, (4) audit for forged tokens in access logs.

scenario: A CSPM compliance check for CloudTrail log file validation is suppressed because the environment tag on the trail is environment=dr (disaster recovery). A suppression rule exempts DR environment resources from audit controls on the assumption that DR resources are passive replicas. However, this CloudTrail covers the active DR environment that is currently serving as the primary environment after a failover 3 months ago — the environment tag was never updated after the failover.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Suppression based on a stale environment tag. After a DR failover, the 'DR' environment became the active primary, but the environment tag and suppression rules were not updated to reflect the new operational reality.
detection_signal: CSPM: CloudTrail 'healthcare-dr-trail' tag environment=dr matches DR suppression rule. CloudTrail log file validation check suppressed. Current state: this trail is the active primary CloudTrail since failover 3 months ago.
ground_truth: Environment has been operating in DR failover mode for 3 months. This CloudTrail is the only active audit trail. Log file validation disabled means CloudTrail logs could be tampered with undetected. HIPAA audit integrity requirement not met.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) enable CloudTrail log file validation, (2) update environment=dr tag to environment=prod-failover, (3) review suppression rules for DR environments to account for DR-as-primary scenarios.

scenario: A GCP SCC finding for a public Cloud Storage bucket containing mental health assessment scores was closed as RESOLVED based on a remediation action taken at 2025-01-20T15:00:00-05:00 (EST). The actual GCP API call to remove the allUsers binding executed at 2025-01-20T20:15:00Z (UTC). The CSPM tool closed the finding 15 minutes after the remediation was scheduled, but the IAM binding removal completed 5 hours and 15 minutes later due to a backlog in the GCP IAM API. A 5-hour window of continued public access was not detected.
why_misclassified: EC-48: Timezone and async operation mismatch. The finding was closed based on when the remediation was initiated, not when GCP IAM API confirmed the binding removal. The async IAM propagation delay created a 5-hour undetected exposure window.
detection_signal: CSPM finding GCP_PUBLIC_BUCKET closed: resolution_time=2025-01-20T15:15:00-05:00 (5 minutes after remediation scheduled). GCP IAM binding removal confirmed: 2025-01-20T20:15:00Z. 5-hour gap.
ground_truth: Mental health assessment scores publicly accessible until 2025-01-20T20:15:00Z. Bucket contained PHI: patient MRN, assessment date, depression/anxiety scores. 5-hour window of public access post-closure.
remediation_impact: Audit GCP storage access logs for 2025-01-20T15:15Z to 2025-01-20T20:15Z for unauthorized reads. Implement remediation verification (confirm GCP IAM binding removed) before closing findings.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a BigQuery table in the clinical analytics project as publicly queryable and tagged phi_scope=true. The table is the primary analytics table used by hospital quality teams and research partners. All patient identifiers have been replaced with pseudonymous tokens using a deterministic tokenization scheme — the token mapping is maintained in a separate, access-controlled BigQuery dataset unavailable to analytics users. The data is tokenized, not raw PHI.
why_misclassified: EC-22: Tokenization compensating control. The scanner detects the phi_scope=true tag and public IAM binding without knowing that all PHI fields have been pseudonymized via format-preserving tokenization. The table contains tokens, not PHI.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: BigQuery table clinical-analytics.patient_outcomes has allUsers bigquery.dataViewer permission. Tag: phi_scope=true. Category: BIGQUERY_TABLE_PUBLIC_ACCESS.
ground_truth: All patient_id, encounter_id, provider_id fields are deterministic tokens. Token vault in bigquery dataset clinical-analytics-tokenmap accessible only to tokenization service SA. Public table contains zero raw PHI.
remediation_impact: Removing public BigQuery access breaks the public health research portal used by 12 university research institutions under a data use agreement.

scenario: Defender for Cloud Identity and Access flags an Azure AD service principal for the HL7 FHIR server as inactive (no sign-ins in 90 days). The service principal is used exclusively for machine-to-machine authentication via client credentials grant — it never performs interactive sign-ins. The last_sign_in_date reflects interactive logins only, not M2M OAuth client credentials flows.
why_misclassified: EC-26: The scanner uses last interactive sign-in date as a proxy for service principal activity without checking OAuth token issuance logs. M2M service principals never have interactive sign-ins but may be highly active via client_credentials flows.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud CSPM: Service principal 'fhir-server-sp' last interactive sign-in: never. Recommendation: disable inactive identity per CIS Azure 1.6.
ground_truth: Service principal used exclusively for M2M client credentials OAuth flow. Azure AD sign-in logs show 1,240 client_credentials token issuances in the last 30 days. Interactive sign-in: not applicable for service principals.
remediation_impact: Disabling the service principal breaks M2M authentication for the FHIR server, halting all EHR-to-FHIR data synchronization workflows.

scenario: GCP Container Analysis flags a HIGH vulnerability in the telehealth video platform container. The vulnerable package (sphinx 7.0.0 with CVE-2023-46341) is a documentation build tool. The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build where the docs stage installs sphinx to generate API documentation during CI. The final runtime image is built FROM a second stage that contains only the video streaming service binary and runtime dependencies.
why_misclassified: EC-43: Build-time documentation dependency flagged as runtime vulnerability. The scanner analyzes all image layers from the build, including the documentation stage that is discarded before the final image is assembled.
detection_signal: GCP Container Analysis: Image telehealth-video-svc:5.0.2 — sphinx 7.0.0 CVE-2023-46341 HIGH. Layer sha256:c4d5... (docs build stage).
ground_truth: Dockerfile stage 1 (docs): FROM python:3.11 — installs sphinx for API docs generation. Stage 2 (runtime): FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12 — COPY --from=builder /app/video-svc. sphinx is absent from runtime image. Runtime image layers: 3 (distroless + app binary).
remediation_impact: Removing sphinx from the docs build stage breaks CI documentation generation. sphinx is not present in the deployed container and poses no runtime risk.

scenario: GCP SCC flags the patient intake form backend service as lacking Cloud Armor protection. The patient intake form application is entirely served through Cloudflare (not GCP Load Balancer directly) — Cloudflare acts as the WAF and DDoS protection layer with OWASP rules and healthcare-specific rate limiting. The GCP backend only receives traffic from Cloudflare's IP ranges.
why_misclassified: EC-16: Edge-shielded by a third-party CDN/WAF (Cloudflare) not detectable by GCP SCC. The scanner only checks for GCP-native Cloud Armor and reports absent Cloud Armor as a gap, without detecting the equivalent Cloudflare WAF layer.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: Backend service 'patient-intake-backend' does not have a Cloud Armor security policy attached. Category: CLOUD_ARMOR_NOT_CONFIGURED.
ground_truth: All traffic routed through Cloudflare WAF (Enterprise plan) with OWASP CRS 3.3, healthcare sector DDoS rules, and IP reputation filtering. GCP backend service ingress restricted to Cloudflare IP ranges only (deny all other sources).
remediation_impact: Adding GCP Cloud Armor behind Cloudflare creates redundant WAF layers with potential rule conflicts and doubles the WAF management surface.

scenario: Microsoft Defender for Containers generates CRITICAL vulnerability findings for a container image in three separate registries: the primary registry (ACR-EastUS), the geo-replicated replica (ACR-WestUS), and a DR registry (ACR-CentralUS). All three registries contain the same image with the same CVE. The CSPM aggregator receives three separate CRITICAL findings for what is effectively one image and one vulnerability, tripling its apparent severity impact.
why_misclassified: EC-38: Cross-region replication duplicate findings. The same vulnerability in a replicated container image generates separate findings per registry. The CSPM aggregator treats them as three independent CRITICAL findings rather than one.
detection_signal: CSPM aggregator: 3 CRITICAL findings for CVE-2023-29491 in image ehr-api:2.0.0 — ACR-EastUS, ACR-WestUS, ACR-CentralUS. Aggregate severity: CRITICAL (3x weight).
ground_truth: Same image, same CVE, replicated across 3 geo-redundant registries for HA/DR. Actual finding count: 1 (one vulnerable image, not three). CSPM must deduplicate registry replicas by image digest before counting findings.
remediation_impact: Patching the image once and pushing to the primary registry will replicate to all three via geo-replication, resolving all three findings simultaneously. The remediation burden is 1x, not 3x.

scenario: Defender for Cloud Identity flags a permanent Global Administrator assignment in Azure AD as a HIGH risk — recommending conversion to PIM-eligible (time-bound) access. The permanent Global Admin is the Break Glass account required by HIPAA §164.308(a)(7) emergency access procedures. The account credentials are stored in a physical safe with dual-custody access controls. Converting it to PIM-eligible access would break the emergency access guarantee.
why_misclassified: EC-28: The scanner cannot distinguish operational Global Admin accounts that should be PIM-eligible from break-glass accounts that require permanent access for disaster recovery compliance.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud CSPM: Azure AD account breakglass@healthsystem.onmicrosoft.com has permanent Global Administrator role. Recommendation: convert to PIM eligible. HIPAA control: AC-6 (Least Privilege).
ground_truth: Break Glass account per HIPAA §164.308(a)(7)(ii)(C) Emergency Access Procedure. Permanent Global Admin required for scenarios where PIM service is unavailable (outage, IdP failure). Dual-custody physical safe controls. Last used: never.
remediation_impact: Converting to PIM-eligible access removes the emergency access guarantee for scenarios where the PIM service itself is unavailable — exactly the conditions when the break-glass account is needed.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a firewall rule on the medical imaging DICOM server as allowing TCP 11112 (DICOM) from a wide source range. The source range is 10.200.0.0/14 — the private IP space used by all 28 radiology departments across the hospital system's campus network, connected via the hospital's private fiber MPLS network. No internet routing exists for this CIDR.
why_misclassified: EC-06: The scanner flags the broad RFC 1918 CIDR range without recognizing it as a private network. 10.200.0.0/14 covers all hospital campus networks connected via MPLS — no internet exposure is possible.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: Firewall rule allow-dicom-campus allows 10.200.0.0/14 on tcp:11112. Category: OPEN_FIREWALL. Severity: HIGH.
ground_truth: 10.200.0.0/14 is the hospital system's private MPLS campus network covering 28 radiology departments. No public internet routing. DICOM MLLP requires broad campus source range for workstation-to-PACS connectivity.
remediation_impact: Restricting DICOM to individual /32 workstation IPs would break imaging connectivity for 340 radiology workstations that receive DHCP addresses within the campus range.

scenario: A multi-cloud aggregator maps an AWS Security Hub MEDIUM finding for cross-account S3 access (allowed by bucket policy to a partner AWS account) to CRITICAL in the risk scoring system. The partner account is owned by the health system's BAA-signed revenue cycle management vendor. The aggregator's CSP-to-risk mapping uses AWS Security Hub's MEDIUM as the base, then over-applies a healthcare multiplier without checking whether the cross-account access is to a BAA-covered entity.
why_misclassified: EC-47: Severity inflation through improper CSP-to-internal severity mapping combined with a blanket healthcare sector multiplier. The cross-account access is to a BAA-covered vendor, making it a permissible business associate access — not a CRITICAL exposure.
detection_signal: Security Hub MEDIUM: S3 bucket policy allows cross-account access from AWS account 987654321098 (RCM vendor). Aggregator applied 2x healthcare multiplier -> CRITICAL.
ground_truth: Account 987654321098 is the revenue cycle management vendor under BAA signed 2024-01-15. Cross-account access is scoped to s3:GetObject on billing/*.claims prefix only. MEDIUM severity at most; CRITICAL is incorrect due to multiplier misapplication.
remediation_impact: Removing vendor cross-account access terminates the automated claims submission workflow, requiring manual submission of 15,000+ monthly claims. BAA compliance requires this access channel.

scenario: GCP SCC flags CVE-2023-22515 (Confluence Server privilege escalation) as HIGH on a GKE node running the clinical workflow automation service. CVE-2023-22515 is a Confluence Server vulnerability affecting Atlassian Confluence — it requires Confluence to be installed and running on the target system. The GKE node runs only containerized clinical workflow services; Confluence is not installed on any GKE node.
why_misclassified: EC-34: Cross-platform/application CVE mismatch. The vulnerability scanner matched the CVE by CVSS score range without validating whether the affected application (Confluence Server) is present. No Confluence installation exists on GKE nodes.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: GKE node 'workflow-node-pool' vulnerable to CVE-2023-22515 HIGH. CVSS 9.8. Workload: clinical-workflow-automation.
ground_truth: CVE-2023-22515 requires Atlassian Confluence Server installation. GKE node OS: Container-Optimized OS (COS). No Confluence installation. Scanner matched CVSS 9.8 to node without verifying affected application presence.
remediation_impact: No patch action possible for a CVE affecting software not installed on the target. Creates false urgency in the remediation queue.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags an RDS snapshot as publicly accessible. The snapshot is a temporary artifact created as part of a quarterly disaster recovery test. The DR test script creates the snapshot, shares it with the DR AWS account (a private cross-account share, not truly public), and deletes it after the restore test completes. Security Hub detected the snapshot during the 12-minute window of the DR test before deletion.
why_misclassified: EC-23: Transient state during a planned DR operation. The scanner detected a snapshot mid-DR-test during a brief window. The snapshot was being shared cross-account (private), not made truly public. Security Hub misclassified cross-account sharing as public.
detection_signal: Security Hub RDS.4: RDS DB snapshots should be private. Snapshot: rds:clinical-prod-postgres-2025-02-01-dr-test. Status: shared.
ground_truth: Snapshot shared only with DR account ID 111122223333 (private cross-account share). Not public. DR test window: 12 minutes. Snapshot deleted after restore test. Security Hub's 'shared' flag misinterpreted as public by CSPM aggregator.
remediation_impact: No action needed — snapshot was deleted as part of DR test completion. DR process is working as designed. CSPM should differentiate between cross-account private sharing and public snapshot sharing.

scenario: An IAM policy finding for a Lambda role with wildcard resource permissions was suppressed 8 months ago during a security exception process. The exception was approved for a 30-day window while a scoped policy was being developed. The exception tag (security_exception=approved) remains on the role and the suppression rule continues to fire. The scoped policy was never implemented, and the role has been accumulating additional wildcard permissions over 8 months.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Time-limited exception that was never expired. The suppression rule has no expiration logic and continues to suppress all IAM findings for roles tagged security_exception=approved regardless of how old the exception is.
detection_signal: CSPM suppression: IAM role 'phi-processor-lambda-role' tag security_exception=approved. All IAM policy findings suppressed. Actual policy: s3:* on *, dynamodb:* on *, ssm:* on *. Exception age: 8 months.
ground_truth: Lambda role has accumulated wildcard permissions across S3, DynamoDB, and SSM over 8 months of development. phi-processor-lambda-role can read/write all S3 objects, all DynamoDB tables, and all SSM parameters in the account. Exception expired 7 months ago.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) revoke security_exception tag, (2) audit CloudTrail for all API calls by this role over 8 months, (3) implement scoped IAM policy, (4) review all roles with security_exception tag for similar expiration failures.

scenario: GCP SCC generates a LOW alert for unusual data access patterns on a Cloud Storage bucket containing genomics research data. A CSPM rule downgrades all data access anomaly findings on research buckets to LOW because research environments have variable access patterns that frequently trigger false positives. The current detection is genuine — an internal researcher's service account has been exfiltrating genomics data (containing patient identifiers) to a personal GCS bucket using gsutil rsync after credential theft.
why_misclassified: EC-50: Overly broad suppression of anomaly findings on research resources. The research access pattern suppression was designed for false positives from legitimate batch jobs but suppresses real exfiltration that matches the 'large data transfer' pattern of legitimate research workloads.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: Anomalous data access on bucket 'genomics-research-prod' — 2.3TB transferred in 4 hours. Suppression rule: research_bucket=true -> downgrade to LOW. Source: SA genomics-researcher-01.
ground_truth: SA genomics-researcher-01 credentials stolen. Attacker using gsutil rsync to exfiltrate 2.3TB of patient genomics data (includes MRN, genetic variants, diagnosis codes). Destination: personal GCS bucket owned by compromised researcher account. Real CRITICAL exfiltration.
remediation_impact: Immediate IR: (1) revoke SA genomics-researcher-01 credentials, (2) remove exfiltrated data from destination bucket, (3) audit GCS transfer logs to determine full exfiltration scope, (4) HIPAA breach notification assessment.

scenario: Amazon Inspector shows zero vulnerabilities for a Lambda function processing prescription data. The Lambda uses a container image that was scanned 30 days ago (clean result). Since then, CVE-2024-6257 (CVSS 7.4, path traversal in the Python grpcio library) was published. The Lambda image has not been rebuilt since the CVE was published, and Inspector only rescans container images when they are pushed to ECR — the image has not been updated.
why_misclassified: EC-24: Stale scan compounded by scan-on-push policy. Inspector only rescans Lambda container images when they are pushed to ECR. A vulnerability published after the last push is never detected unless the image is rebuilt and pushed.
detection_signal: Amazon Inspector: Lambda function 'prescription-processor' container image — 0 CRITICAL, 0 HIGH (last scan: 30 days ago). grpcio 1.54.0 present. CVE-2024-6257 published 18 days ago.
ground_truth: Lambda container image contains grpcio 1.54.0 vulnerable to CVE-2024-6257 (path traversal). CVE published 18 days after last image push. Inspector scan-on-push policy means the vulnerability was never scanned. Image has not been rebuilt.
remediation_impact: Immediate: rebuild Lambda container image with grpcio >= 1.62.0, push to ECR (triggers Inspector rescan), redeploy Lambda. Review Inspector continuous scanning policy for Lambda container images.

scenario: A CSPM check for Azure Key Vault soft delete and purge protection was disabled in the scanner configuration after a version upgrade introduced a bug that generated false positives for all Key Vaults with custom soft-delete periods (non-default 90 days). The buggy check was disabled globally. An attacker who has compromised a Key Vault contributor role is deleting and purging encryption keys for PHI-encrypted S3 equivalents (Azure Blob Storage with CMK). Without purge protection, keys are permanently deleted.
why_misclassified: EC-03: Disabled scanner check creating a systematic blind spot. The Key Vault soft-delete/purge protection check was disabled to suppress false positives from a scanner bug, creating a blind spot for purge protection policy enforcement.
detection_signal: CSPM scanner: KEYVAULT_PURGE_PROTECTION_CHECK disabled (config: skip_kv_purge=true). Attacker deleting and purging CMK keys from key vault 'phi-encryption-kv-prod'. No CSPM finding generated.
ground_truth: Attacker with Key Vault Contributor role is executing az keyvault key delete and az keyvault key purge on CMK keys. Without purge protection, keys are immediately and permanently deleted. PHI-encrypted blobs become permanently unrecoverable.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) enable emergency Key Vault access lockdown, (2) check if any keys were purged (audit KV audit logs), (3) re-enable KEYVAULT_PURGE_PROTECTION_CHECK with proper false-positive fix, (4) assess data recoverability.

scenario: GCP SCC downgrades a HIGH finding for a GKE pod with metadata server access (IMDS) to LOW because it detects GKE Workload Identity is enabled on the cluster and applies a Workload Identity compensating control. However, the specific pod running the legacy medication reconciliation service has the annotation iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account not set and is using the default Compute service account — Workload Identity is enabled at cluster level but not configured for this specific pod, which still accesses IMDS with the default service account.
why_misclassified: EC-31 analog: compensating control applied at cluster level without verifying per-workload configuration. Workload Identity enabled at cluster level does not guarantee all workloads are using it — pods without the annotation still use the default Compute SA via IMDS.
detection_signal: CSPM: GKE pod 'med-reconciliation-legacy' IMDS access finding downgraded LOW: GKE Workload Identity detected as cluster-level compensating control. Pod annotation iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: not set.
ground_truth: Pod med-reconciliation-legacy accesses IMDS using default Compute service account (project-default@developer.gserviceaccount.com). Workload Identity not configured for this pod. Default Compute SA has roles/editor on the healthcare project.
remediation_impact: Immediate: configure Workload Identity for med-reconciliation-legacy pod with a least-privilege SA. Review all GKE pods missing iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account annotation to identify other Workload Identity gaps.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags a publicly accessible S3 bucket used by the hospital's medical education department. The bucket contains medical case studies used for resident training. All case studies were authored by clinical educators using synthetic patient profiles generated by Synthea — no real patients. The bucket is public to enable medical students to access learning materials without AWS credentials.
why_misclassified: EC-21: Synthetic data used for medical education. The scanner flags the bucket as phi-adjacent due to the clinical content tag, but the case studies use entirely synthetic patients. The bucket is intentionally public for educational access.
detection_signal: Security Hub S3.2: S3 bucket 'medical-education-cases-prod' public read access. Tag: content_type=clinical_cases.
ground_truth: All 840 case studies use Synthea-generated patient profiles. No real patient data. Bucket serves as a public medical education resource. Clinical educator oversight confirms synthetic-only content policy.
remediation_impact: Restricting the bucket would prevent 250+ medical residents and students from accessing required training materials, impacting clinical education programs.

scenario: Defender for Containers flags CVE-2024-21626 (runc container escape) as HIGH in an AKS pod running the patient scheduling service. The CVE was subsequently disputed by the Red Hat Security Response Team who published a VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability Exchange) statement indicating that the specific runc binary in Red Hat's UBI9 base image was compiled with a flag that prevents exploitation of this particular code path. The scanner does not consume VEX statements.
why_misclassified: EC-46: Withdrawn/disputed CVE based on VEX attestation. The Red Hat UBI9 compilation flag makes the CVE unexploitable in this specific binary, but the scanner's database still lists the CVE as HIGH without VEX awareness.
detection_signal: Defender for Containers: AKS pod 'patient-scheduling-svc' — runc 1.1.9 CVE-2024-21626 HIGH. Image base: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal.
ground_truth: Red Hat VEX statement RHSA-2024:0724: runc in UBI9 compiled with RHEL hardening flags that prevent exploitation of CVE-2024-21626. VEX justification: COMPONENT_NOT_PRESENT (specific code path disabled). Defender does not consume VEX attestations.
remediation_impact: Rebuilding the image to upgrade runc to a 'fixed' version that Red Hat hasn't released yet would destabilize the OCI runtime with no security benefit given the VEX attestation.

scenario: A CSPM tool flags a DynamoDB table used by the pharmacy management system as having an overpermissive resource policy allowing access from multiple AWS accounts. The table stores only pharmacy transaction tokens — the actual prescription data is stored in a separately encrypted RDS instance. The tokens in DynamoDB are surrogate keys with no pharmaceutical or patient value without the prescription data they reference.
why_misclassified: EC-22: Tokenization at the DynamoDB layer. The scanner sees cross-account DynamoDB access on a pharmacy-tagged table and assumes PHI risk. The table contains only surrogate tokens (format-preserving tokens for prescription IDs) with no standalone sensitivity.
detection_signal: IAM Access Analyzer: DynamoDB table pharmacy-transaction-tokens has resource policy allowing access from accounts [111122223333, 444455556666] (pharmacy benefit managers). Table tagged: phi_scope=true.
ground_truth: DynamoDB stores format-preserving tokens only: prescription_token -> maps to prescription_id in encrypted RDS. Tokens have no PHI value without the RDS mapping table. Cross-account access is for authorized PBM claims processing under signed BAAs.
remediation_impact: Restricting DynamoDB access breaks automated claims submission workflows with the pharmacy benefit management companies that have signed BAAs.

scenario: Defender for Cloud flags a Cosmos DB account used by the care coordination platform as not using a customer-managed key. The platform's application layer encrypts all PHI fields (patient demographics, care plan details, contact information) using Azure SDK field-level encryption with keys stored in Azure Key Vault before writing to Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB stores only encrypted ciphertext for all PHI attributes.
why_misclassified: EC-13: Application-layer field-level encryption compensates for absent Cosmos DB CMK. The scanner inspects Cosmos DB's native CMK configuration without knowing about the application-layer encryption applied before data insertion.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: Cosmos DB account 'care-coordination-cosmos-prod' does not have customer-managed key configured. HIPAA control: DP-5.
ground_truth: All PHI fields encrypted via Azure SDK EncryptionCosmosClient using Key Vault key 'care-coord-phi-key' before Cosmos DB write. Cosmos DB stores Base64-encoded ciphertext for: patient_name, dob, contact_info, care_plan_details. AES-256 applied at application layer.
remediation_impact: Enabling Cosmos DB CMK while application-layer SDK encryption is active results in double-encryption with no PHI benefit. Would require migrating 450GB of existing encrypted documents.

scenario: Amazon Inspector flags CVE-2022-3602 and CVE-2022-3786 (OpenSSL 3.x critical vulnerabilities) as CRITICAL in the clinical decision support service container. The container is built on a distroless base (gcr.io/distroless/base-nossl-debian12) which explicitly excludes libssl and libcrypto. The 'nossl' distroless variant was chosen specifically to eliminate OpenSSL attack surface. The CVE match is a false positive from Inspector incorrectly inheriting vulnerability metadata from a parent image layer.
why_misclassified: EC-29: Distroless 'nossl' variant has no OpenSSL libraries. The scanner matched the CVE to the image based on the Debian base layer without detecting that the 'nossl' distroless variant explicitly excludes all OpenSSL components. The image contains zero OpenSSL binaries.
detection_signal: Amazon Inspector: Image cds-service:3.0.1 — CVE-2022-3602 CRITICAL, CVE-2022-3786 CRITICAL. Base: gcr.io/distroless/base-nossl-debian12.
ground_truth: distroless/base-nossl-debian12 explicitly excludes libssl1.1, libssl3, libcrypto-related packages. Image contains no OpenSSL libraries (confirmed by docker run --rm cds-service:3.0.1 find / -name 'libssl*' 2>/dev/null: no output). CVE match is erroneous.
remediation_impact: There is no OpenSSL to patch in a nossl distroless image. The finding is a scanner artifact from incorrect CPE matching on the Debian base layer metadata.

scenario: An RDS MySQL instance hosting patient intake forms was given a suppression exemption tag (exempt=maintenance) during a network reconfiguration 6 weeks ago. The reconfiguration was supposed to move the instance to a private subnet but the Terraform apply failed silently on the subnet association step. The RDS instance remains publicly accessible (publicly_accessible=true with a resolvable DNS endpoint and permissive security group). The maintenance exemption tag continues to suppress the public access finding.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Time-limited maintenance exemption that was never removed after the failed remediation. The Terraform apply appeared to succeed in CI logs (non-zero exit code suppressed), but the subnet association step silently failed, leaving the instance exposed.
detection_signal: CSPM suppression: RDS instance 'patient-intake-mysql-prod' tag exempt=maintenance. Finding RDS_PUBLIC_ACCESS suppressed. Current state: publicly_accessible=true, security group allows 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0.
ground_truth: RDS instance patient-intake-mysql-prod: publicly_accessible=true, DNS endpoint resolvable from internet, security group sg-0mysql-intake allows 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0. Contains patient intake form data: name, DOB, insurance ID, chief complaint. 6-week exposure window.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) restrict security group 3306 to application tier SG only, (2) remove exempt=maintenance tag, (3) fix Terraform subnet association, (4) audit MySQL slow query logs for unauthorized access, (5) conduct HIPAA breach risk assessment.

scenario: A CSPM tool shows a PHI archive S3 bucket as compliant for KMS CMK encryption. The bucket's KMS key was scheduled for deletion 30 days ago as part of a key rotation, and the deletion schedule completed at 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z (UTC). The CSPM tool's finding was marked COMPLIANT at 2024-12-31T16:00:00-08:00 PST (= 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC) — exactly when the key was deleted. The CSPM cache retained the last-compliant state, and no new non-compliant finding was generated because the bucket CMK check polls at 24-hour intervals.
why_misclassified: EC-48 + EC-24: Timezone coincidence at key deletion time combined with 24-hour polling interval. The CMK was deleted at the exact moment the CSPM marked it compliant (due to timezone display), and the next poll 24 hours later found the bucket now using default AWS encryption (key deletion degraded it silently).
detection_signal: CSPM: S3 bucket phi-archive-prod showing COMPLIANT for CMK encryption (cached state from 2024-12-31). Actual state: KMS key arn:aws:kms:...:key/abc123 in PendingDeletion status, then Deleted. Bucket reverted to SSE-S3 (default key).
ground_truth: KMS CMK deletion completed 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z. Bucket phi-archive-prod: SSEAlgorithm now aws:kms with default AWS key (not CMK). PHI archive is no longer encrypted with customer-managed key. 24-hour polling gap missed the transition.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) create new KMS CMK, (2) re-encrypt bucket objects with new key, (3) reduce CMK encryption check polling to 1 hour for HIPAA-scoped buckets, (4) validate KMS key deletion impact assessment process.

scenario: A CSPM IAM privilege escalation check was globally disabled 4 months ago when a scanner update generated mass false positives for all roles using AWS-managed policies. A developer who left the organization retained an IAM role (via a personal access key never revoked after offboarding) and has been exfiltrating patient records from S3 using the broad permissions of their former data analyst role. The disabled IAM check means no privilege analysis findings are generated for this account.
why_misclassified: EC-03: Disabled scanner check creates a persistent blind spot exploited by an insider threat (former employee with active credentials). The check was disabled globally due to upgrade FP issues and never re-enabled with proper tuning.
detection_signal: CSPM scanner: IAM_PRIVILEGE_ESCALATION_CHECK disabled (config: skip_iam_analysis=true). Former employee access key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE active, using data-analyst-role to perform s3:GetObject on phi-records-prod. No IAM finding generated.
ground_truth: Former data analyst employee's IAM access key never revoked during offboarding (HR-IT disconnect). Key has been used 234 times in the past 30 days to download patient records from S3. CloudTrail shows consistent after-hours access from residential IP.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) revoke access key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE, (2) disable data-analyst-role, (3) audit all S3 GetObject calls from this key over the past 4 months, (4) HIPAA breach notification assessment, (5) re-enable IAM privilege check with proper tuning.

scenario: A GCP firewall rule allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 is tagged with owner=platform-team and has been suppressed because platform team resources require broad SSH access per their operational model. The rule was added 11 months ago to a healthcare application VPC by a developer who copied it from a platform team playbook. The application VPC serves the telehealth patient database and the SSH rule was never part of the approved network design.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Tag-based suppression based on an unauthorized tag application. The owner=platform-team tag was copied from a playbook and applied to an application VPC resource that does not belong to or require platform team SSH access patterns.
detection_signal: CSPM suppression: firewall rule 'allow-ssh-any' in VPC telehealth-patient-vpc tag owner=platform-team. SSH open finding suppressed. Actual: healthcare application VPC, not platform team VPC.
ground_truth: Firewall rule allow-ssh-any allows 0.0.0.0/0 on tcp:22 in telehealth-patient-vpc. VPC hosts telehealth patient database server (PostgreSQL with PHI). SSH from internet to database server. Rule not approved in network design review. 11-month exposure.
remediation_impact: Immediate: delete allow-ssh-any firewall rule in telehealth-patient-vpc. Audit GCP audit logs for SSH connections from non-corporate IPs. Implement IAP (Identity-Aware Proxy) for any legitimate SSH access needs.

scenario: Defender for Cloud shows a PHI document storage account as compliant for diagnostic logging. An Azure region outage 45 days ago caused the diagnostic settings for the storage account to be reset to default (logging disabled) during a failover. The Defender assessment for this storage account has not refreshed since before the outage due to a Defender plan renewal lapse of 2 weeks. PHI access has been unlogged for 45 days.
why_misclassified: EC-24: Stale assessment. Defender plan renewal lapse caused a 2-week gap in assessments during which the outage-triggered configuration reset went undetected. The cached pre-outage compliance state shows COMPLIANT.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: Storage account 'phi-documents-prod' diagnostic logging: COMPLIANT (last assessment: 47 days ago, pre-outage). Current state: StorageRead/Write logging disabled (reset during regional failover).
ground_truth: Storage account phi-documents-prod: StorageRead logging disabled since 2025-01-01 (post-outage reset). 45 days of PHI access (read/write operations on patient consent forms, lab reports) are unlogged. HIPAA audit trail gap.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) re-enable diagnostic logging for StorageRead, StorageWrite, StorageDelete, (2) notify privacy officer of 45-day audit trail gap, (3) review Defender plan renewal process to prevent future assessment lapses.

scenario: A GuardDuty finding for UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce was suppressed 14 months ago when an EC2 instance running SSH on a non-standard port (2222) generated repeated false positives from legitimate bastion jump server access. A suppression rule was applied to all SSH brute force findings on instances tagged role=bastion. A different EC2 instance (the EHR application server) was incorrectly tagged as role=bastion during a Terraform variable substitution error, and is now actively being brute-forced from a foreign IP with the finding suppressed.
why_misclassified: EC-49: Tag-based suppression applied to an incorrectly tagged resource. The role=bastion tag was accidentally applied to the EHR application server via a Terraform variable error. GuardDuty findings on this host are suppressed despite it being the application tier, not the bastion.
detection_signal: GuardDuty: UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce on i-0ehr-app-prod-02. Suppression: tag role=bastion matches SSH brute force suppression rule. Active attack: 4,200 failed SSH attempts from 185.220.x.x (Tor exit node) in 10 minutes.
ground_truth: EC2 i-0ehr-app-prod-02: EHR application server (incorrectly tagged role=bastion due to TF variable error). Active SSH brute force from Tor exit node. Instance has database credentials in /etc/app/config. PHI database accessible.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) block source IP, (2) restrict SSH to bastion-only SG, (3) correct Terraform role=bastion tag, (4) review all role=bastion tagged instances for correctness, (5) rotate database credentials on affected instance.

scenario: GCP SCC shows a Cloud SQL instance hosting patient records as compliant for automated backups. A Cloud SQL maintenance update 50 days ago introduced a bug that silently disabled automated backups on instances with custom backup windows outside business hours. The compliance check reflects the pre-update state from 55 days ago (last assessment). Patient records have had no automated backup for 50 days.
why_misclassified: EC-24: Stale assessment. The SCC compliance check runs every 7 days but the backup state was changed by a maintenance update between assessments. The maintenance bug caused a silent backup disable not detected until the 7-day polling cycle caught the new state — but the CSPM tool had a cached result showing COMPLIANT.
detection_signal: GCP SCC: Cloud SQL instance patient-records-db-prod automated backups: COMPLIANT (last check: 55 days ago). Current Cloud SQL API: backupConfiguration.enabled=false (maintenance regression).
ground_truth: Cloud SQL patient-records-db-prod: automated backups disabled since maintenance update 50 days ago. 50 days of no backup. HIPAA requires backup and disaster recovery capabilities per §164.308(a)(7). Last available backup: 50 days old.
remediation_impact: Immediate: (1) re-enable Cloud SQL automated backups, (2) trigger on-demand backup immediately, (3) verify backup integrity, (4) report to compliance team as HIPAA contingency plan gap.

scenario: Defender for Cloud flags 12 AKS worker node VMs as lacking endpoint protection. The VMs are Azure Container-Optimized OS (AKS) nodes that run only containerized workloads — no traditional applications. The hospital deploys CrowdStrike Falcon for Containers as the container security solution, which provides runtime threat detection at the container level. CrowdStrike is deployed as a DaemonSet on all AKS nodes but uses a different detection model than traditional endpoint AV.
why_misclassified: EC-05: WAF/endpoint protection shielded architecture — the scanner looks for Microsoft Defender for Endpoint or standard AV agents and finds none, without detecting the CrowdStrike Falcon container DaemonSet providing equivalent protection at the container runtime layer.
detection_signal: Defender for Cloud: AKS node VMs aks-nodepool1-* missing endpoint protection solution. Severity: HIGH. HIPAA control: SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection).
ground_truth: CrowdStrike Falcon for Containers deployed as DaemonSet on all 12 AKS nodes. Provides runtime container threat detection, drift prevention, and process behavior monitoring. CrowdStrike agent not recognized by Defender's endpoint inventory.
remediation_impact: Deploying Defender for Endpoint alongside CrowdStrike on AKS nodes would create agent conflicts and double the security agent resource overhead on Kubernetes worker nodes.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags an EKS cluster's public API server endpoint as a HIGH risk. The EKS cluster is in the staging environment which uses only Synthea-generated synthetic patient data for integration testing. The public endpoint enables developer access from home offices during CI/CD testing without requiring VPN. The staging environment has no PHI and is outside the HIPAA BAA scope.
why_misclassified: EC-09: The scanner applies production-level severity to a staging EKS cluster without considering environment context. Staging with synthetic data and public EKS API server is a common and acceptable developer experience trade-off when no PHI is involved.
detection_signal: Security Hub EKS.1: EKS cluster control plane should not be publicly accessible. Cluster: ehr-integration-staging. endpointPublicAccess: true.
ground_truth: Cluster ehr-integration-staging: environment=staging, hipaa_baa_scope=false, data_type=synthetic. Public endpoint required for developer access from home offices during remote CI/CD test runs.
remediation_impact: Disabling public endpoint for a staging cluster requires developers to use VPN for all kubectl access, significantly slowing iteration speed for a non-PHI environment.

scenario: Security Hub flags an SQS queue used in the medication order processing pipeline as not using a KMS CMK for server-side encryption. The queue carries medication order messages, but the application layer encrypts all PHI fields (patient_id, medication_name, dosage) using AWS Encryption SDK before enqueuing. Messages in SQS contain only encrypted ciphertext. The queue's default SQS-managed encryption (SSE-SQS) provides a second encryption layer over the already-encrypted message payloads.
why_misclassified: EC-13: Application-layer AWS Encryption SDK encryption is not visible to the SQS encryption scanner. The scanner checks the SQS QueueAttributeName SqsManagedSseEnabled or KmsMasterKeyId without knowing that all messages are pre-encrypted before enqueue.
detection_signal: Security Hub SQS.1: Amazon SQS queues should be encrypted at rest using SSE. Queue: medication-order-pipeline-prod. KmsMasterKeyId: null.
ground_truth: All SQS messages encrypted with AWS Encryption SDK (AES-GCM 256) before enqueue. Message payload is ciphertext only. SSE-SQS (AWS-managed) provides a second encryption layer over already-encrypted ciphertext. No plaintext PHI ever reaches SQS.
remediation_impact: Adding KMS CMK to SQS while application-layer encryption is active adds unnecessary KMS API calls and key management overhead with no additional PHI protection.
